$schema_note: User-visible product improvements, newest first. Feeds the pipeline's What's-new card and the homepage footer's latest-improvement stamp — one source, both surfaces (the homepage must match the real site). Keep entries honest, dated, and user-phrased; trim to ~12.

entries.title: What the loan does over the hold, and the refinance at the end
entries.blurb: A payment tells you nothing about what you still owe. $13M at 6.5% over thirty years, held ten, leaves $11.02M at the balloon — a third of the schedule has run and 85% of the loan is still there. /tools now draws every year's debt service split into interest and principal, so the widening principal sliver shows what amortisation actually is: equity, paid in instalments and returned at sale, not a cost. Under it the balloon feeds a take-out test sized on the same three lender tests as any loan — cash out, covers it, or the cash-in refinance nobody plans for, with the NOI that would clear it.

entries.title: What the lease is really worth, and one expense three ways
entries.blurb: Every office and industrial rent in a memorandum is a STARTING rent, and the gap to net effective is where the broker's number lives. $36 a foot on a ten-year deal with twelve months free and $90 of tenant improvements is not $36 a foot — /tools now draws where the face rent actually goes, and gives both net effective figures, the straight-line one most memoranda quote and the discounted one that charges the landlord for waiting. Plus one operating expense said per unit, per foot and as a share of income, because a broker quotes the first and an underwriter argues the third.

entries.title: A sizing is a link, and a table is a paste
entries.blurb: “Send me that sizing” used to mean a screenshot. Every field on /tools now writes itself into the address bar, so the whole page — all five calculators — travels as a link, and an untouched page still copies as a bare /tools rather than a paragraph of defaults. The cash-flow table copies tab-delimited with its headers and the numbers raw, so they land in a spreadsheet as numbers instead of as text somebody has to clean.

entries.title: Paste a cash flow, get the IRR — and where it came from
entries.blurb: The most common reason an analyst leaves a screening tool mid-call is to paste a column of numbers into Excel and read the IRR off the bottom. /tools now takes that column — tabs, line breaks, (1,200), $1.2M, all of it — and answers with the rate, the multiple, the profit and the payback inside the year. Then the figure nothing else here computes: how much of the return is the sale rather than the operations. A 17% that is three-quarters residual and a 17% that is a quarter are different deals wearing the same number.

entries.title: One recorded sale is no longer called a median
entries.blurb: The public-records comps readout printed “1 recorded sales — median $400,000 · range $400,000–$400,000” and then a confident percentage against it. One sale is a data point, not a market. The figure still shows — it is the only evidence there is — but it is named correctly, the range is dropped where there is nothing to range over, and the above/below call is withheld until there are enough sales to have a middle.

entries.title: The market photographs are actually visible now
entries.blurb: Fifteen skylines shipped this morning and then rendered at about an eighth of their strength, under a wash nobody had measured. The picture now draws at full strength and the scrim does the work — dark under the words at the bottom of a band, clearing until the city is most of what you see. The contrast is computed against a pure white frame, the worst photograph a market could have, so it can never quietly slide back.

entries.title: The deal math reads what you actually type
entries.blurb: Typing $20M into a price field used to yield nothing at all — a page of em dashes for a perfectly ordinary number. Every field on /tools now reads the shorthand an analyst uses: $20M, 500k, 1.2mm, 6.5%, 1.25x, and a negative NOI, which is a real thing to put into a debt sizer.

entries.title: Deal math you can run before there is a deal
entries.blurb: Size a loan against LTV, debt service coverage and debt yield and see which one actually binds — that is the half of the answer a bare number leaves out. Plus the cap rate triangle, yield on cost against the exit cap, and one rent said four ways. It all runs in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere.

entries.title: Fifteen markets get the photograph they are known by
entries.blurb: Washington opens on the Mall, Miami on Brickell, Philadelphia on the Schuylkill River. Every file, photographer and licence was read back from Wikimedia Commons by the deploy probe rather than written from memory, and each deploy re-checks that all fifteen still resolve.

entries.title: Every market picture becomes a photograph of the place
entries.blurb: A market is known by its skyline, not by its roofs. Each covered market now draws a real skyline photograph where one is verified, with the photographer and licence named beside it, and keeps its overhead frame only as the floor. A deal still shows its own site from above — that roof is the asset.

entries.title: Each market brief opens on its own downtown
entries.blurb: Pick a market on /market and the brief opens on that market from above — the same public-domain USGS frame the homepage gallery draws for it — as a band carrying the region and the market's name. The picture is the place whose rules, rents and benchmarks follow.

entries.title: The sign-in page opens on a real place
entries.blurb: Baltimore's Inner Harbor from above stands behind the sign-in card — the last public page that opened on a flat colour — a public-domain USGS frame under the same scrim, credited in the corner.

entries.title: Every public page opens on a real place
entries.blurb: The homepage's hero, the argument on /why and the sample screen on /demo each open on a real photograph of a covered downtown — Midtown Manhattan, Washington, and Center City Philadelphia, the sample deal's own city — public-domain USGS frames under a scrim, credited in the corner.

entries.title: A real photograph behind the homepage's headline
entries.blurb: Midtown Manhattan from above — a public-domain USGS frame, the same source as the coverage gallery — now stands behind the hero, under a scrim that keeps the type readable, with its credit in the corner. Four slots wait for ground-level photographs (a team on deal day, a site walk, the building itself, a hero of your own) and show nothing until the files exist — never a placeholder.
